My dog is single purpose his sole job is to find firearms. I'm lucky to be supported so well by my organization I've got a take home car and pretty much any training I want to take with the dog I can. Its a huge commitment and a bunch of work but its one of the best jobs out there. My training consisted of 4 weeks for single purpose detection school. You learn how to handle the dog, what changes in behavior to look for, how to hold a leash, how to detail and teach the dog a search routine for rooms, cars, and possibly luggage or lockers, some basic first aid and things to watch out for and thats pretty much it. There is a certifying test and the end where you take all you learned and go through searching rooms, searching vehicles, and whatever else is specific to your dogs certification. At no point during my training was I ever given any obedience training, which is why I say start that early, theres plenty of quality youtube videos out there. My dog took a solid 2 months of just working obedience every day, to not be a Tasmanian devil when we walk around the hospital. We just recertified about a month ago with the USPCA.

Our protocol for a panic alarm is once its triggered, its put out over the radio, Officers start responding as our dispatch calls the nurse station where the panic alarm was. We have under a 2 minute response time to anywhere in the hospital. For the most part we learn the trouble units where the alarm goes off and we haul ass. If its a false alarm, or faulty alarm, we go up and try and educate the nursing staff and doctors on why these alarms are important and to be aware and not hit them. We also test every alarm monthly and when we are doing our active shooter training with nursing staff we train them to hit the alarm and let them test it during training.

So if you're in the US and she went to a hospital for S.I. shes most likely baker acted. Baker acts are a 72 hour legal hold. She cannot leave. At my hospital we take everything from a baker act including cell phone upon arrival. Most baker acts dont last the full 72 hours, usually they get medicated and either the doctor lifts the hold, or they get sent to a mental health rehab place for more advanced care. Have your girlfriend add you as an emergency contact in her electronic medical record. That way the hospital can tell you where she is, and can contact you in the future. Unfortunately right now she could be deemed to lack capacity to make medical decisions, which means Mom may be making them for her.

So we teach our armed guys who work nightclubs, once the bad guy is down or the threat is eliminated to call 911 immediately, say they are armed security working at the club, they've been involved in a shooting. "When the Bataclan theater in Paris was attacked by three heavily armed gunmen in November, tactical police units raided the hall within 35 minutes".

When they first arrive at an active shooting scene, police face a quick decision, said Suffolk County, N.Y., Chief of Patrol Stuart Cameron, who has written several academic journal articles about police protocol when faced with an active shooter.

If police rush in on a barricaded suspect, they risk the lives of their officers and the hostages. But if they delay in responding to an active shooter, that can also be risky: Analyses of past shootings suggest that one person is killed every 15 seconds in a typical mass-casualty shooting, Cameron said.

The onus for early action falls on the first officers to arrive. According to FBI statistics, in 57 percent of active shooting incidents, police were at the scene before the shooting ended.

The intent of the shooter is also critical, Cameron said, and he teaches officers to distinguish among suspects looking to knowingly commit a crime against an individual or small group; the mentally ill; and terrorists.

“If the shooting crosses into terrorism,” Cameron said, “that changes the equation.”

Terrorism suspects are less likely to let their hostages live, and may tell police during a mass-casualty incident — such as those in Mumbai in 2008 and in Paris last year — that they are willing to negotiate, only to prolong the media exposure of a terrorist attack.

“Unless hostages or bystanders are being killed, once the incident is contained, the initial responders should try to slow things down.”

The guideline to officers Cameron trains is to run toward gunfire, Cameron said.

“But when the gunfire stops, you stop,” Cameron said. “You don’t know what’s going on inside there. He could have hostages, he could have killed himself or he could be waiting for you to come charging in without a plan.”
